title: (Scenario) A race condition causes the SAME payment to be processed twice — how do you prevent it end to end (idempotency key per request, a unique DB constraint on the transaction id, transaction management, a distributed lock only where truly needed, atomic operations), and crucially how do you handle client/payment-provider RETRIES so a retry returns the original stored result instead of charging again?
shortTitle: (Scenario) A race condition causes the SAME payment to be processed twice — how do you prevent it end to end

s1_definition.profdef: You prevent double processing end to end with layered defenses: an idempotency key per request so the server recognizes a repeat, a unique database constraint on the transaction id so the database itself refuses a second row atomically, proper transaction management so the business change and the idempotency record commit together, atomic compare-and-set operations to claim the key, and a distributed lock only where the contended resource is not a database row you can constrain. Retries from the client or the payment provider are handled by returning the stored result for a known key rather than performing the charge again.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh pays, the bank stamps his request with a unique ticket number. If the same ticket comes back, whether because Rajesh's phone retried or the card network retried, the clerk looks up the ticket, sees it was already handled, and hands back the exact same receipt instead of charging him again. The ledger also physically refuses two entries with the same ticket number, so even if two clerks act at the same instant, only one entry can exist.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stop double charges with an idempotency key the server can recognize, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the atomic last line of defense, and a transaction that commits the charge and the key together, so any retry returns the stored result instead of charging again.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You prevent double processing end to end with layered defenses: an idempotency key per request so the server recognizes a repeat, a unique database constraint on the transaction id so the database itself refuses a second row atomically, proper transaction management so the business change and the idempotency record commit together, atomic compare-and-set operations to claim the key, and a distributed lock only where the contended resource is not a database row you can constrain. Retries from the client or the payment provider are handled by returning the stored result for a known key rather than performing the charge again.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh pays, the bank stamps his request with a unique ticket number. If the same ticket comes back, whether because Rajesh's phone retried or the card network retried, the clerk looks up the ticket, sees it was already handled, and hands back the exact same receipt instead of charging him again. The ledger also physically refuses two entries with the same ticket number, so even if two clerks act at the same instant, only one entry can exist.

**One line to remember:** Stop double charges with an idempotency key the server can recognize, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the atomic last line of defense, and a transaction that commits the charge and the key together, so any retry returns the stored result instead of charging again.

sections.s2_technical:
First understand the race. Two requests for the same logical payment arrive almost simultaneously, perhaps the client timed out and retried while the first was still in flight, or the payment provider retried its webhook. Both check "has this payment been processed?", both see no, and both proceed to charge. The window between the check and the write is where the race lives, so the fix must make the check-and-claim atomic and must have a hard backstop even if the application logic races.

The outermost layer is the idempotency key per request. The client generates a unique key for the logical payment and sends it on every attempt including retries. The server uses this key as the identity of the operation. The critical implementation detail is that claiming the key must be atomic: you do not read-then-write in two steps, you attempt a single atomic insert of the key with an in-progress status. If the insert succeeds you are the first and you proceed; if it fails with a duplicate-key error, someone else owns this operation, so you either return their stored result or, if they are still in progress, wait or return a conflict. This single atomic claim closes the check-then-act window.

The hard backstop is a unique database constraint on the transaction id or payment reference. Even if two threads somehow both believe they are first, the database will allow only one row with that transaction id; the second insert fails atomically. This is the guarantee you can actually trust under concurrency because it is enforced by the database, not by hopeful application code. You catch the duplicate-key exception and treat it as "already processed", then return the existing result.

Transaction management ties it together. The charge, the ledger update, and the idempotency or transaction record must commit in the same database transaction, so you can never end up with money moved but no record, or a record but no money. If the transaction rolls back, both disappear and the client can safely retry. Atomic operations like a conditional update, for example `UPDATE payments SET status='DONE' WHERE id=? AND status='PENDING'`, give you single-winner semantics inside the database without a separate lock.

A distributed lock is used only where truly needed, which is when the contended resource is not a database row you can constrain, for example a one-time external coupon or a rate-limited external gateway slot. For an ordinary payment keyed by transaction id, a unique constraint is cheaper and safer than a distributed lock, so you do not reach for a lock by default.

Finally, handling retries so a retry returns the original result. Once the first request completes, you store the full response, status and body, against the idempotency key. Any subsequent request with the same key, whether from the client, a proxy, or the payment provider, is detected and the stored response is returned verbatim without charging again. The senior nuances are: give idempotency records a TTL appropriate to the retry window; handle the in-progress case explicitly so a retry arriving before the first finishes does not double-charge, typically by making the second caller wait on the row lock or return 409 so the client retries later; make the key scope correct so it identifies the logical operation, not the HTTP attempt; and remember the same discipline applies to asynchronous consumers, where at-least-once delivery is just another source of retries that a processed-id check must absorb.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's app timed out mid-payment and retried while the first request was still processing, and both requests charged him, so he paid twice. This is exactly why the idempotency-key claim must be a single atomic insert, so the second request cannot also believe it is first.

Problem 2 — Even with the key check, a true thread race slipped two charges through once. This is exactly why we add a unique constraint on the transaction id as a hard database backstop that only one row can satisfy.

Problem 3 — The payment provider retried its confirmation webhook, and the system must return the original result rather than re-charge. This is exactly why we store the response against the key and replay it on any retry.

Our mini-project builds a payment service hardened against the race. The code defines a `PaymentRequest` with an idempotency key, a `PaymentStore` that atomically claims a key and enforces a unique transaction id, a `PaymentService` that charges inside a transaction-like critical section and stores the response, and a demo that fires two concurrent requests with the same key to prove only one charge happens, then simulates a provider retry that returns the stored result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one logical payment with idempotency key IDEM-RAJESH-77 and transaction id TXN-77, fired by two concurrent threads, then retried once by the provider.

Step 1: Both threads are released at the same instant and both call `claimKey("IDEM-RAJESH-77")`. Because the claim is an atomic put-if-absent, exactly one thread gets true and the other gets false. The race is resolved at the claim, not at a separate check.

Step 2: The winning thread inserts the unique transaction id TXN-77, which succeeds, then records the charge, builds the response, and completes the key by storing the response and marking it DONE.

Step 3: The losing thread, having failed the claim, sees the key is in progress, waits briefly until it becomes DONE, and then returns the stored response. It never charges.

Step 4: The charge counter shows exactly one, proving that despite two concurrent requests only one charge was applied.

Step 5: The payment provider retries the same request later. The claim fails because the key exists and is DONE, so the service immediately replays the stored response without charging, and the counter stays at one.

```
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Performed charge for TXN-77
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    RACE result A = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    RACE result B = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77 (replayed after wait)
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Total charges applied for TXN-77 = 1
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    PROVIDER retry = CHARGED SAV2001 Rs.50000 txn=TXN-77 (replayed stored result)
2026-10-24 14:17:40 INFO    Total charges after provider retry = 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Same payment: key=IDEM-RAJESH-77, txn=TXN-77  (fired by 2 concurrent threads)
    │
    ├── Thread A ─┐                 ├── Thread B ─┐
    ▼             ▼                 ▼             ▼
  claimKey(IDEM-RAJESH-77)  ← ATOMIC putIfAbsent → only ONE wins
    │ A: TRUE (first)                 │ B: FALSE (loser)
    ▼                                 ▼
  insertUniqueTxn(TXN-77) ✓       state == DONE? wait → replay stored
    │ (hard DB backstop)              │
    ▼                                 ▼
  recordCharge() → charges=1       return stored response (NO charge)
    │ complete(key, response)
    ▼
  charges = 1  ✓ single charge

  ── Provider retry (later) ──
  pay(req) → claimKey FALSE, state DONE → replay stored response → charges still 1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The first thing I do with this scenario is name the race precisely: two requests for the same logical payment arrive almost simultaneously, often because the client timed out and retried while the first was still in flight or the payment provider retried its webhook, both check whether the payment was processed, both see no, and both charge. The window between that check and the write is where the double charge is born, so my whole design is about collapsing that window and adding a hard backstop that holds even if the application logic races.

The outermost defense is an idempotency key per request that the client sends on every attempt including retries, and the crucial implementation detail is that claiming the key must be a single atomic operation, not a read-then-write. I attempt one atomic insert of the key; if it succeeds I am the first and I proceed, and if it fails as a duplicate, someone else owns the operation, so I either replay their stored result or, if they are still in progress, wait on the row or return a conflict. The hard backstop beneath that is a unique database constraint on the transaction id, because even if two threads somehow both think they are first, the database allows only one row with that transaction id and the second insert fails atomically. That database-enforced guarantee is the one I actually trust under concurrency, not hopeful application code.

I bind these together with transaction management, committing the charge, the ledger update, and the idempotency or transaction record in the same transaction so I can never end up with money moved but no record or a record with no money, and if it rolls back both vanish and the client can safely retry. I use atomic conditional updates for single-winner semantics inside the database, and I reach for a distributed lock only where the contended resource is not a database row I can constrain, like a one-time external coupon, because for an ordinary payment a unique constraint is cheaper and safer than a lock. Then the retry handling falls out naturally: once the first request completes I store the full response against the key, and any later request with the same key, from the client, a proxy, or the provider, is detected and the stored response is replayed verbatim without charging again.

On my project at National Bank of India this came from a real incident where Rajesh's app retried mid-payment and he was charged twice, and later a genuine thread race slipped two charges through. We hardened the flow with an atomic idempotency-key claim as an insert, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the database backstop, the charge and the record committed in one transaction, and the full response stored against the key so provider webhook retries replay the original result. The explicit in-progress handling, where a second concurrent request waits or gets a 409 rather than double-charging, was the detail that finally made the concurrent case safe.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I prevent a double charge end to end with an atomic idempotency-key claim, a unique constraint on the transaction id as the hard database backstop, and a single transaction that commits the charge and the record together, so every client or provider retry returns the stored result instead of charging again, and I only add a distributed lock when the scarce resource is not a row I can constrain.
